sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

arguments.content:
# 🏄 Surfing Pelican

An animated, non-interactive 3D scene of a pelican surfing an endless swell,
built with plain [three.js](https://threejs.org/) — no assets, everything is
generated in code.

## What's in the scene

- **Shader ocean** — a vertex-displaced plane driven by a table of sine waves.
  The exact same wave table is used in JavaScript to compute the water height
  and analytic surface normal, so the surfboard truly rides the swell, banking
  into slopes and weaving across the water.
- **Procedural pelican** — built from primitives: plump body, long curved neck,
  big yellow beak with a wobbling orange throat pouch, spread wings that flap
  for balance (with feathered tips), crouched orange legs on webbed feet, and a
  head that looks around.
- **Surfboard** — extruded bezier outline with a red stripe and fin.
- **Spray** — point-sprite water spray kicked up around the tail of the board.
- **Atmosphere** — gradient sky dome, sun disc with specular glint on the water,
  drifting flat-shaded clouds, distant banking seagulls, and a slow cinematic
  orbiting camera.

## Files

- `index.html` — entry point (title overlay + canvas)
- `main.js` — the whole scene (ES module, imports `three` from npm)

## Run locally

```bash
npm install
npx serve .   # or any static server, then open index.html
```

The page is fully offline-capable and uses no storage or network requests.

content.text:
Done. Everything is in the current directory:

- **`index.html`** — entry point with a title overlay and full-screen canvas, loading `main.js` as an ES module.
- **`main.js`** — the full scene, importing `three` from npm:
  - **Shader ocean**: a 220×220 displaced plane driven by a table of 5 sine waves; the identical wave table is used in JS to compute water height + analytic normal, so the surfboard genuinely rides, banks, and leans with the swell.
  - **Procedural pelican** (all primitives): plump white/grey body, curved neck, big yellow beak with a wobbly orange throat pouch, eyes with glints, spread wings that flap for balance with feathered tips, crouched orange legs and webbed feet, head that looks around, wagging tail.
  - **Surfboard**: extruded bezier outline with red stripe and fin; the rig weaves across the water and leans into turns.
  - **Extras**: point-sprite spray kicked up at the board's tail, gradient sky dome, sun disc with specular glint, drifting clouds, five distant banking seagulls, soft shadows that follow the surfer, and a slow cinematic orbiting camera.
- **`README.md`** — short description and run instructions.
- Installed `three` via npm; `npx esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` succeeds (~1.2 MB bundle).

No interactivity, no network/storage use — it's a pure animated diorama that runs offline in a sandboxed iframe.
